单说原著向的Sara和Becky的话这绝对是我今年玩到的最纯粹澄澈的百合线，但是本游戏里制作组塞入的改编Jessie线和Lavinia线又能把我气死，好吧当场切割。
Sara绝对是我目前为止见过的最值得被爱的女主角，虽出身高贵被宠爱着长大却平等待人、良善又爱憎分明、温和又保有自己思虑、好学博识、乐观积极、耐心开朗……简直是含着金汤勺出生、亮晶晶的宠儿，仿佛被天使吻过被仙女祝福过。
但宠儿的命运并没有一直被眷顾，父亲破产与死亡的消息在Sara生日的那天带走了她的一切。“朋友”的亲近、校长Minchin女士的讨好与恭维、女仆Mariette、优秀学生的地位、优越的生活条件、尊严……全都离Sara而去。从最被他人关注艳羡的小千金沦落为被嘲弄打压奴役的仆从，天堂到地狱不过如此。
重要的剧情转折，关系到各个结局分支。在被改编的路线中，Jessie线和Lavinia线简直槽点满满，爱Sara？不！她们只是爱自己！


Jessie是一位有着漂亮的外观可家境不算太好的女孩，她很清楚自己很容易面对被家里人嫁给自己不爱的人的命运——所以她攀附他人，她寻求“强者”的庇护，她不仅攀附着Lavinia这棵大树，她还试图投资Sara这棵有潜力的小树。
她既不敢完全背叛Lavinia，对于落难的Sara也有些许同情，她若即若离。被安排订婚、在知道Lavinia不会给她带来庇护后她向Sara抛出一起叛逃出走的邀请，你说她是很想带Sara一起离开吗，才不是呢！我只觉得她是想抓一个同伴逃避命运，高贵的Lavinia不会理睬她不会是她叛逃的同伴，但落难的Sara可能是。
可Sara现实，拒绝了邀请。Jessie没有找到叛逃的同伴也没有勇气赴死，只能接受订婚的命运，改编剧情中她吻了Sara又赠送了像征自己心意的心型项链。
这是爱吗？我觉得不是，这太可笑了！Minchin女士以心型项链为由诬陷Sara的时候她都不曾出面！
她是菟丝子，渴望他人的力量，她只在乎自己，在乎她的梦想、自由与美丽。

Lavinia更是一位爱自己到极致的让人生厌的角色，我完全不理解制作组为何一心将她做成可选爱情线。
她打一开始就不喜欢Sara，看不起Sara，用生硬、刻薄的话语抵制她。在得知Sara将拥有钻石矿后，Lavinia不再是Minchin女士最“得意青睐”的学生，她也不再是学生里最受关注的那个，她的顶尖地位受到了挑战，她嫉恨Sara。这种情绪在Sara从云端掉落到泥泞后爆发了，Lavinia如愿以偿地回到了最顶端的位置，她践踏侮辱俯视Sara好似能从中获得一些安慰与快感——因为她也具有印度血统，但她极端嫌恶自己的血脉，所以她努力让自己在各方面显得高人一等，这样的行为好像能抹除她心中那点低劣。
Lavinia线感情的发展居然是因为Sara得知了她印度的血统并表明自己也有，她当即表明Sara与自己是相似的，Sara能理解自己，不允许Sara离开她，她爱她。
我十分困惑于这个发展，难道Lavinia不会更加恼羞成怒——你与我都有着低贱的印度血脉，凭什么你一直高贵端庄得像个公主。
这当然也不是爱，自始至终Lavinia都是从上方俯视着Sara的，即使是“求爱”，她也强势、傲慢，态度几近施舍。Lavinia这家伙的当务之急是学会尊重人，将别人（Jessie）称作宠物的人真的懂爱吗。
而且比起说是求爱，Lavinia更像是在找一份能让自己心安的理由，一个同一阵营的同伙——看，我们虽然都有印度血脉，但我们非常高贵。
她是从污浊之地移植走的玫瑰，她享受他人的崇拜与赞美，排斥自己过去的污秽。她只在乎自己，在乎她的高贵与华丽。

痛斥了一通终于要说回原作里的Becky线了，或许正因为是原作情节，剧情很顺畅细腻。
Becky是学院的小女仆，地位处于本作的最底层，Sara以友善平等的态度对待她埋下了善因，这在之后Sara成为女仆后结下了善果。Becky不会低看落魄的Sara，一位在高位时都愿意赠予他人关怀的小姐即使失去了一切，她的心灵也比其他所有人都高贵。
二人在Sara最艰难的时期算是一个比较平等的的关系。Sara也一直在告知认为自己低贱的Becky每个人都是一样的，每个人都可以成为自己的公主。两个小小的人在寒冷的夜晚拥簇在破旧寒冷的阁楼里，分享着破旧的被子与体温——这在其他人的剧情线里是没有的，没有人能做到共患难，她们的身份很高她们也没有足够的勇气去抵抗Minchin女士的权威。在她们的线里即使有后续的转折，我也只感觉实际的Sara毫无希望、孤苦无依地死在了那个破旧寒冷的阁楼上，后续Sara爸爸的朋友带着财富收养她显得那么渺茫与理想化。
Becky的存在实在是很好地缓冲了我的悲伤。我也很高兴地看到这条线里Sara虽遭受命运打击却依旧明亮乐观，会继续编缀她美丽的童话，会勇敢地与Becky一起直面Minchin女士，会在教堂Becky要掉下去时紧紧地抓着她的手，果断而用力地说 我会、我一定、我有信心把你拉回来，你不能离开。
在前面的故事中我一直认为Sara是一位虽然懂事温和，心里却像小鹿一样执拗灵动的孩子，不然也不会阳奉阴违在背地里偷偷腹诽她所不认可的话。其他的路线或多或少我都看到了Sara接受命运变得屈服顺从，但Becky线她没有，她依旧倔强、直率、纯真却有力量。
我也觉得教堂Sara拉住Becky这段剧情有点影照整体剧情的意思，是两个人的互相扶持与不离不弃换来的奇迹。Sara一直坚定地决定把Becky“拉上来”，摆脱“深渊”。
二人的结局就很顺其自然啦，衔接上Sara父亲的朋友收养她、Sara重新拾回财富与地位，请求Becky的爱希望带她走的结局，很顺畅与美满。这也是所有路线中Sara唯一一条主动意识到自己的感情并且主动去表白的。两个善良的小姑娘值得获得最好的结局。

如果还要说什么不满，那就是制作组偏心也太厉害了，Sara和Becky的结局cg有点崩，制作组是不是收了Lavinia的贿赂啊，打完后还在“奖励”模块专门额外多给一张Sara和Lavinia在床上极显暧昧的图片。奖励什么？奖励Lavinia是吧。。。游戏直至结束也没有惩罚Minchin这个恶毒势力的女人，也不曾出现后日谈云云。
切割吧。我要去看原著了。（无怜悯）

A Little Lily Princess, developed by Hanabira and published by Hanako Games, is a thoughtful and heartfelt visual novel that reinterprets the classic story of A Little Princess through interactive storytelling and gentle yuri romance. Drawing inspiration from Frances Hodgson Burnett’s original novel, the game places players in the role of Sara Crewe, a bright and imaginative young girl sent from India to attend a London boarding school. While the foundation of the story follows the familiar arc of privilege, loss, and resilience, this adaptation expands upon the emotional relationships within the setting, allowing players to shape Sara’s bonds with those around her in meaningful ways.

The narrative begins with Sara arriving at the seminary as a wealthy and adored student, nicknamed a “little princess” because of her background and demeanor. Early chapters focus on establishing friendships, adjusting to the school’s routines, and navigating subtle rivalries among classmates. However, tragedy soon disrupts her comfortable life, and Sara’s social standing collapses overnight. Forced into servitude within the same institution where she was once admired, she must endure hardship while maintaining her compassion and dignity. This transition forms the emotional backbone of the story, exploring themes of perseverance, kindness, and inner strength.

Unlike purely linear visual novels, A Little Lily Princess incorporates light stat-raising and scheduling mechanics that add an element of strategy to the experience. Each in-game week allows players to choose Sara’s activities, such as studying, working, or spending time with certain characters. These decisions influence her statistics and determine which events become available. This structure encourages careful planning and experimentation, as building certain attributes or prioritizing particular relationships unlocks new scenes and route developments. While the overarching plot remains recognizable, the individual character arcs can vary significantly depending on player choices.

The romance routes are a central feature of the adaptation, offering six potential companions whose relationships with Sara can evolve beyond friendship. Each character brings a distinct perspective and emotional dynamic. Some routes highlight loyalty and long-standing camaraderie, while others delve into unlikely alliances formed through shared adversity. The romantic elements are handled with sensitivity and restraint, focusing on emotional connection rather than overt dramatics. The result is a series of heartfelt stories that emphasize trust, understanding, and mutual growth.

The character writing stands out as one of the game’s strongest elements. Sara herself is portrayed as imaginative and empathetic, retaining her resilience even in the face of humiliation and hardship. The supporting cast is equally layered, with personalities that range from warm and supportive to insecure or antagonistic. Even characters who initially appear one-dimensional are given opportunities for growth and nuance, especially through the branching routes. This depth enriches repeat playthroughs, as players gain a fuller understanding of each character’s motivations and vulnerabilities.

Visually, the game adopts a soft anime-inspired art style that complements its Victorian setting. Character sprites are expressive, and event illustrations add emphasis to pivotal emotional moments. Backgrounds capture the atmosphere of the boarding school and surrounding London streets, reinforcing the period tone without overwhelming the narrative focus. The soundtrack features gentle compositions that enhance the emotional beats of the story, creating a consistent and immersive mood.

While the scheduling system adds replay value, it can occasionally feel unpredictable, as certain events depend on stat thresholds or random outcomes. This may require multiple attempts to unlock specific routes or endings. However, for many players, this element of uncertainty mirrors the unpredictability of life itself and enhances the sense of accomplishment when a desired outcome is achieved. The presence of multiple endings further encourages exploration, making each playthrough feel like a new perspective on the same foundational tale.

Ultimately, A Little Lily Princess succeeds as both a respectful homage to its literary source and a fresh reinterpretation that centers on character agency and emotional intimacy. It transforms a familiar story of hardship into a branching narrative rich with friendship and romance, allowing players to shape Sara’s journey toward happiness. For fans of character-driven visual novels, historical settings, and gentle yuri romance, it offers a layered and emotionally resonant experience that balances classic storytelling with interactive depth.

This is a charming little yuri vn, and I liked the life that the (very light) management mechanics gave to the gameplay (especially since there's no choices to be made here beyond who you choose to romance) but as a huge fan of the original book, the story left me feeling pretty hollow. 

One of the great strengths of the book is the emotional connections that Sara forms, which sustain her through some absolutely dreadful experiences. And a lot of what makes this game shine is how it expands upon those relationships--every character in this game is in the original novel, but many of them have a very small role in the story. The devs have turned each of these characters into full, three-dimensional people, each with her own life and story and relationship with Sara. And the first act of the game is full of these lovely friendships--you get to have one event per week with the character of your choice (assuming you have the stats for it), and the game outright advises you to focus on two or three at the most, as you won't have time to befriend everyone. Even taking this advice, you will have an event every week, stats permitting, and you might not finish all the routes.

The second half, however, is eerily empty. You'll have an event with everyone you befriended in the first act, and then there will be a well-signposted event whose selection will lock you into a character's romance route. Once you're locked to a romance route, the other characters don't speak to you again, even in the game's main story, even platonically. It's jarring to have these friendships you built evaporate overnight, doubly so for the characters whose routes are explicitly non-romantic. And the act two routes don't have enough events to fill even half the weeks in that act. The game thus gets lonely, grindy, and a hair boring in spite of Sarah's budding romance. It would have greatly benefited from shorter, platonic routes that can be played alongside the romance, even if you can only select one of each.

Well this was absolutely lovely. 
All of the girls were lovely and their routes were all very interesting, my only real complaint is that I wish there was more development for each girl. I'm very impressed they managed to make Lavinia likeable in her ending, in fact it was probably my favourite.
The relationship between Sara and each girl is varyingly romantic or more ~close feelings~ and I actually found that quite nice, The variety was rather pleasant and fit the broader yuri exploration of "feelings between girls" rather than 100% romance. 
There's some rather orientalist elements that no doubt are a holdover from the book but I felt they weren't particularly egregious and they were "period appropriate" so to speak without being terribly unpleasant. 

All-in-all this was a really delightful experience and definitely one that I was sad to have to put down once it was over.

That said, the writing is good, the art is engaging and if you like the genre, it is worth picking up.

A Little Lily Princess is an adaptation of one of my childhood favourite books, A Little Princess by Frances Hodgson Burnett, best known as the author of The Secret Garden. It imagines Sara Crewe and almost all of the supporting characters as lesbians, which I enjoyed as a lesbian who always seeks lesbian representation in the media I consume. This is one of the adaptations that stays closest to the overall story of the original novel, while carefully adding in fuller backstories for each of the supporting characters.

Sara Crewe is a sheltered, wealthy heiress born and raised in India, but like many English children at the time, sent away to boarding school when she becomes old enough that it's expected. Her father dies after abruptly losing his entire fortune, and she's turned into an indentured servant at the boarding school to repay the debts her father had to the seminary. She's gentle and kind, and strives to remain so despite the poor treatment she's put through at the hands of Miss Minchin, the seminary's headmistress. 

Each route focuses on Sara's relationship with a different person in her world, from her former classmates, to her lady's maid, to a motherless younger child Sara took on a nurturing role with. Some of the routes are romantic, but they're very chaste and innocent, respecting the characters' young ages. There's no hint of romance whatsoever in the relationships Sara has with her much older maid or much younger school friend. Those relationships are purely mentoring and familial. 

The adaptation includes more diversity than you'd expect from a game set in the Victorian era, having multiple mixed characters and characters of different racial backgrounds. It also gently pokes holes in some of the casual racism from the original novel, like Sara wondering why English children have to be sent away from India due to the "poor climate" while Indian children seem to do fine there. One character's route focuses a lot on internalized racism. There's also one character whose story focuses a lot on what she experiences as a specifically lesbian young woman, and I felt that story was told very well. 

I've played the game to completion, and have replayed it more than once to re-read a specific character's route. I particularly enjoyed Jessie and Mariette's routes. 

There's very little difficulty in this game compared to something like Long Live the Queen. You can't die, you can't even really miss a route you're set on going down. The only choices you make that influence the story are choosing which character's route to go down, and it's easy to replay and go down all six routes, thus seeing every aspect of the game. It's relaxing to play because of this. I really enjoyed the music of the game as well.

This was such a delightful VN; I was moved to tears a number of times.

A Little Lily Princess tells a beautiful story of hope, kindness, and resilience -- while also managing to largely avoid the problematic implications Cinderella-like stories can sometimes have. Emotional suppression is not glamorized, and I can see that care was taken to make it clear that one's lot in life is not determined by what one "deserves" (i.e., bad circumstances don't mean you're a bad person, and good circumstances don't mean you're above those less fortunate).

Each of the routes was very good. It was a relief to see the creators be sensitive to the cast's ages -- not all routes are romantic, and even the routes that are never go beyond a chaste kiss as far as getting physical. As such, it manages to thoroughly avoid becoming creepy. I think the only negative thing I'd say about the entire game is that I felt like some of the routes ended very abruptly; it would have been nice to have an epilogue or something. But at the same time, that's also somewhat fitting for the story, for us to simply imagine (or "suppose," as Sara would say) what might happen after the ending of the game, so I don't mind it too much.

I particularly enjoyed the music. I felt it set the tone well, without being distracting during intense scenes. The art is also beautiful, especially in the CGs.

The controls are easy to grasp, and the RNG for determining your daily character stat increases is entirely reasonable. I focused on only one route at a time and found that I didn't actually need to "save scum" at all. I didn't encounter any type of glitches or anything while playing. The in-game checklist is nice, too. It has all the features you'd expect from a VN, such as music replay and a gallery.

As a visual novel, the time to complete the game is going to vary a lot based on your reading speed, and whether you re-read or skip previously read sections. I played through the whole thing quickly enough I didn't need to review things I'd already read and am a fast reader, but How Long to Beat indicates I finished quite a bit faster than most. Even with having finished it so fast, though, A Little Lily Princess was completely worth it to me.

The story takes place over the course of 36 weeks separated into two acts. At the beginning of each week, you can choose a focus for a side story. Shortly after act 2 begins, you lock in a side story that determines one of the six endings.

Overall, I liked the story and I liked going through the different endings, though I do think that the second act was rushed; things just wrapped up far too quickly and neatly. But there are certainly some touching moments and I'm glad I read through this story. I also thought the music was quite nice but as for CG, the art is very good but there aren't very many pictures; only 21, six of them chibi.

First, I did read the book and see the movie, but it's been so long I barely remember it, so I can't speak to how much it captures the feel of the source content. However, on its own, the game is very sweet and enjoyable.
 
The routes vary in how romantic they are. Two are not romantic at all (one involving a character much younger and one a character much older than MC) and involve a more familial dynamic. Due to the setting and the age of the characters, there is very little explicit discussion of the nature of the characters' relationships, with only one character outright saying they like women, but the relationships feel appropriate for the story and were still very cute (no spoilers, but I in particular loved the ending CG for Becky's route).

The MC feels a little too perfect at times, but the other characters are much more rounded out, and some especially have some complex themes in their routes. 

I enjoyed the writing and the way it felt more like reading an actual novel, but be aware it is very text-heavy. The random elements of the stats could feel a bit irritating at times, but it rarely became a true issue and the game alerts you when routes are about to be locked off. 

The art is very nice, though there is one outfit that the MC wears that, while very cute, feels really out of place and is used more than once, making it kind of distracting. 

I'd say depending on how quickly you read, you'll probably get a few hours out of the initial playthrough, with the additional routes maybe taking another hour or so with the text skip turned on (ignore my playtime, I left the game running woops).

Overall, I really recommend this for fans of sapphic stories, especially those looking for something more focused on the overall relationship and not just the romantic tension. I honestly wish more games like this were out there.

A very cute Edwardian era novel with minimal, but still some management gameplay elements. The story is based on a well regarded children's novel of the period, and so the writing, setting, and characterization is all very accurate and better than you find in most visual novels, though it can be a bit cloying at times. I do have one complaint though,  the gameplay allows the game to be split up into multiple routes, which is what is expected out of most visual novels. However, many of the routes could be considered to be simultaneous, so it feels like you have to replay them all to get a complete picture of the story. I feel that with only a couple exceptions, and a handful of details needing to be changed, that they could all have been combined into one larger more complete story, and that would've been a more satisfying experience. Still, I enjoyed my time with this visual novel and do recommend it.
